mainTopic: Which statues count as עבודה זרה, what objects in their hands signify, and whether found fragments are permitted
overview: The amud opens with רבה limiting the משנה's dispute about statues. His first version says the argument is only about village statues. The גמרא objects that village statues are obviously made for worship. So it restates his teaching: the argument is about city statues, which might be decorative, and village statues are forbidden by everyone. The גמרא then explains that a staff, bird, or orb in a statue's hand shows the idol's claimed rule over the world. A ברייתא adds a sword, a crown, and a ring to that list. For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, even a pebble or a twig in the hand is enough. רב אשי asks about a statue holding excrement, and the question stays unresolved (תיקו). A new משנה permits found broken pieces of statues but forbids hand or foot shapes. שמואל extends the permission even to pieces of a real idol, and the גמרא begins to challenge him from the hand-and-foot ruling, a challenge that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבה limits the dispute to village statues
steps.stepSummary: רבה says רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue only about statues in villages. Statues in cities are permitted by everyone, because they are made for decoration.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: The argument is about statues in villages. But statues in cities are permitted according to everyone. Why? Because people make them for decoration.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה tells us where the משנה's argument applies. He says it is only about village statues, and that city statues are permitted by everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is that city statues are put up as decoration (נוי), not for worship. If the argument is about village statues, then the חכמים must permit some village statues, as if those too might be decorative. The next step attacks exactly this point.

keyTerms.meaning: a dispute; here between רבי מאיר and the חכמים

phrases.english: Rabba said:
The dispute is about those of villages,
phrases.notes: "The dispute" means the argument in the משנה between רבי מאיר and the חכמים about statues.

phrases.english: but regarding those of large cities,
everyone agrees they are permitted.
What is the reason?
They make them for decoration.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new limitation on the scope of the משנה's dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: First version: the dispute is about village statues, and city statues are permitted by everyone because they are decorative.

steps.title: Village statues are surely made for worship
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how anyone could permit village statues, since no one would think they are made for decoration.
steps.simpleTranslation: And about village statues, is there anyone who says they make them for decoration? Village statues are certainly made in order to worship them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה's version. If the חכמים permit some village statues, they would have to think those statues are decorative, and that makes no sense.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In villages nobody puts up statues just to look nice. They are put up for worship. So it is hard to say the חכמים would permit village statues, and the limitation in step 1 cannot be right as stated.

keyTerms.meaning: is there anyone who says…? (asked with surprise)

phrases.english: And regarding those of villages, is there anyone
who says they make them for decoration?
Those of villages are certainly
made in order to worship them!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִכְפָרִים, מִי אִיכָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לְנוֹי קָעָבְדִי לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the logic of רבה's first version.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the dispute is about village statues.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the חכמים permit village statues, they must think those statues are decorative. But village statues are obviously made for worship, so no one could permit them.

steps.title: רבה's statement restated: the dispute is about city statues
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the report of רבה's words. The dispute is about city statues, and village statues are forbidden by everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said: רבה said: The argument is about statues in cities. But statues in villages are forbidden according to everyone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by swapping the cases. It says רבה actually taught that the argument is about city statues, while village statues are forbidden by everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: City statues could have been made for decoration, so there is room to argue: רבי מאיר forbids them all, and the חכמים permit them unless they hold a staff, bird, or orb. Village statues are clearly made for worship, so everyone agrees they are forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, if it was said, this is how it was said (a correction of how a teaching was reported)

steps.whatToRemember: The final version of רבה's teaching: the dispute is only about city statues, which might be decorative. Village statues are forbidden by everyone.
steps.confusionAlert: The word אלא here does not mean רבה changed his mind. The גמרא is saying his words were passed on wrongly, and this is what he really said.

phrases.english: Rather, if it was stated, this is how it was stated:
Rabba said: The dispute is about those of large cities,
but regarding those of villages,
everyone agrees they are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge by restating רבה's teaching the other way around.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the version of a teaching (swapping which cases are in dispute).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dispute is about village statues, and city statues are permitted by everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is about city statues, and village statues are forbidden by everyone.

steps.title: Why a staff, bird, or orb shows the statue is an idol
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the חכמים in the משנה and explains that the staff, bird, and orb each show the idol's claimed rule over the whole world.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: And the חכמים say: They are forbidden only if the statue holds a staff, a bird, or an orb. A staff means it rules the whole world like someone ruling with a staff. A bird means it holds the whole world like someone holding a bird. An orb means it holds the whole world like someone holding a ball.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns back to the משנה and quotes the opinion of the חכמים. Then it explains what each object in the statue's hand stands for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each object stands for power over the whole world. A staff stands for ruling it, and a bird or a ball stands for holding it in one's hand. A statue holding one of these is presented as a god, so the חכמים say it was made for worship and is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the חכמים's test in the משנה: a statue is forbidden only when it carries a sign that it claims to rule the world.

phrases.english: "And the Rabbis say: They are only forbidden, etc."
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. The "etc." stands for the rest: only statues holding a staff, a bird, or an orb.

phrases.english: A staff: because it rules itself
phrases.notes: "Itself" is a roundabout way of putting it. He means the idol rules the whole world.

phrases.english: under the entire world, as with a staff.
A bird: because it grasps itself
under the entire world, like a bird.
An orb: because it grasps itself
under the entire world, like a ball.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה to explain the symbols named in the חכמים's opinion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A staff, a bird, and an orb each stand for the idol's claimed rule over the whole world, so a statue holding one of them is made for worship.

steps.title: A ברייתא adds three more items: sword, crown, and ring
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that three items were added to the חכמים's list: a sword, a crown, and a ring.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: They added to the list a sword, a crown, and a ring.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds three more items to the משנה's list of things that show a statue is an idol. This sets up the next step, which explains each item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed a staff, a bird, and an orb. The ברייתא says the list was later made longer. A statue holding or wearing a sword, a crown, or a ring is also treated as an idol and is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: They added to them (to the earlier list)

phrases.english: It was taught: They added to them:
phrases.notes: "Them" means the staff, bird, and orb that the חכמים listed in the משנה.

phrases.english: a sword, a crown, and a ring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the explanation of the משנה's list by bringing a ברייתא that makes the list longer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sword, a crown, or a ring on a statue also marks it as an idol.

steps.title: Why each added item was first ignored and later counted
steps.stepSummary: For each item, the גמרא explains the harmless first impression and the later understanding that it shows the idol's claimed rule over the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sword: At first they thought it merely showed a bandit. In the end they understood it means the idol claims it can kill the whole world. Crown: At first they thought it was merely a woven wreath. In the end they understood it as a royal crown. Ring: At first they thought it merely showed a seal-bearer. In the end they understood it means the idol claims it can seal the whole world for death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why these three items were not on the original list and why they were added later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item has two possible meanings. At first each looked ordinary: a robber's weapon, a simple wreath, an official's seal. Later the חכמים saw that each one, like the staff, bird, and orb, shows the idol claiming power over the whole world. That is why they were added.

keyTerms.meaning: A seal-bearer, an official with a signet ring

steps.confusionAlert: "Kills itself" and "seals itself" do not mean the idol hurts itself. The גמרא uses a softer way of speaking so it does not say outright that the world will be killed.

phrases.english: A sword: at first they thought
it was merely a bandit,
but in the end they thought

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהוֹרֵג אֶת עַצְמוֹ תַּחַת כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ.
phrases.english: that it kills itself under the whole entire world.
phrases.notes: He means the idol claims it can kill the whole world. "Itself" is a gentler way of saying it.

phrases.english: A crown: at first they thought
it was merely a woven wreath,
but in the end they thought it was like a crown of a king.
phrases.notes: Literally "for a dog." The גמרא uses an insulting word instead of "king" when it speaks about an idol.

phrases.english: A ring: at first they thought
it was merely a seal-bearer,
but in the end they thought that it seals itself
under the whole entire world for death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind each item the ברייתא added in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each added item, like the original three, shows the idol's claimed power over the whole world. That is why it marks the statue as an idol.
steps.whatToRemember: An item makes a statue an idol when it shows a claim to rule over the whole world. The sword, crown, and ring were added once the חכמים saw they carry that meaning.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: even a pebble or a twig
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבן שמעון בן גמליאל from the משנה and brings a ברייתא: even a pebble or a twig in the statue's hand makes it forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says (any statue with anything in its hand is forbidden). It was taught in a ברייתא: Even a pebble, even a twig.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next opinion in the משנה, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, and brings a ברייתא showing how far his view reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים forbid a statue only when it holds items that show rule over the world. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל forbids a statue holding anything at all. The ברייתא makes this concrete: even a worthless pebble or twig is enough.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the real gap between the two views. For the חכמים, the meaning of the item matters. For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, any item in the hand is enough.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, etc.
phrases.notes: This points back to the משנה, where he says a statue with anything at all in its hand is forbidden.

phrases.english: It was taught: even a pebble,
even a twig.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל כּוּ׳. תָּנָא: אֲפִילּוּ צְרוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the חכמים's list to the next opinion in the משנה, that of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, a statue holding anything, even a pebble or a twig, is forbidden.

steps.title: רב אשי asks about a statue holding excrement
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks whether a statue holding excrement is forbidden, since the excrement could be read two opposite ways.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: if the statue holds excrement in its hand, what is the law? Do we say it means the whole world is worthless to it, like excrement? Or perhaps it means the statue itself is worthless to the whole world, like excrement?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds one more item to the list of things held in a statue's hand, and asks if it makes the statue forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier items, like a staff or a ring, showed the idol's claimed power, so they made the statue forbidden. Excrement is unclear. If it shows that the idol looks down on the world, it fits that pattern and is forbidden. If it shows that the idol is itself disgraced, then nobody is honoring it, and it is not forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (an open question, not an attack)
Do we say... or perhaps... (setting out two possible ways)

phrases.english: Rav Ashi asked:
If it holds excrement in its hand, what is the law?
Do we say

phrases.aramaic: כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא זִילוּ בְּאַפֵּיהּ כִּי צוֹאָה,
phrases.english: that the whole world is worthless in its eyes, like excrement,
or perhaps

phrases.aramaic: הוּא מִיהוּ דְּזִיל בְּאַפֵּי כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא כְּצוֹאָה?
phrases.english: it itself is worthless in the eyes of the whole world, like excrement?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the list of objects held in a statue's hand (staff, bird, orb, sword, crown, ring, pebble, twig) to an unclear case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does excrement in the statue's hand show that the idol looks down on the world, so the statue is forbidden, or that the idol itself is disgraced, so it is not?

steps.title: The question stays unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves רב אשי's question without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand: the question remains unanswered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes רב אשי's question without deciding it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source settles which of the two readings of the excrement is correct. So the question is left open, and the topic of objects in a statue's hand ends here.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question remains unanswered

steps.whatToRemember: A statue holding excrement is an unanswered question (תיקו): it may show contempt for the world, or disgrace for the idol itself.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question raised in step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The law about a statue holding excrement stays undecided.

steps.title: משנה: broken statue pieces are permitted, but hand or foot shapes are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that broken pieces of statues may be used, but a shape of a hand or foot may not, because such shapes are worshipped.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who finds broken pieces of statues may use them. If he found the shape of a hand or the shape of a foot, they are forbidden, because things like them are worshipped.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives two rules about objects someone finds: broken statue pieces are allowed, and hand or foot shapes are forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A random broken piece is not something people worship, so it is permitted. A hand or foot shape is different: people do worship objects like that on their own. So even a hand or foot shape found by itself is treated as a possible idol.

keyTerms.meaning: Permitted / forbidden (here: to use or benefit from)

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who finds broken pieces of statues,
these are permitted.
If he found the shape of a hand
or the shape of a foot,
these are forbidden,
because things like them are worshipped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה about found fragments, after the discussion of whole statues.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Found statue fragments are permitted, but a found hand or foot shape is forbidden, because such shapes are worshipped.

steps.title: שמואל: even pieces of a real idol are permitted
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the permission covers even broken pieces of something known to be עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: שמואל said: even broken pieces of an actual idol are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with שמואל, who stretches the משנה's permission to pieces of a known idol, not just a regular statue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה spoke about 'statues', which might not have been worshipped. שמואל adds that even if the pieces came from a real idol, they are still permitted. This sets up the challenge that comes next.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Shmuel said:
Even broken pieces of an idol are permitted.
phrases.notes: The word 'permitted' is not in the text; שמואל is continuing the משנה's 'these are permitted.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֲפִילּוּ שִׁבְרֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Broken pieces of an actual idol are permitted.

steps.title: But the משנה only said 'statues'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל: the משנה said 'statues', which suggests pieces of a real idol would be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: 'broken pieces of statues'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל using the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה meant that even idol pieces are allowed, it should have said 'idol pieces'. Saying 'statues' seems to show that only plain statue pieces are allowed, which goes against שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: But we learned (in a משנה)! An attack from a source

phrases.english: But we learned:
"broken pieces of statues"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's statement from the משנה's wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that even pieces of an actual idol are permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה chose the word 'statues', which suggests only pieces of non-worshipped statues are permitted, not pieces of a real idol.

steps.title: The word 'statues' was chosen to set up the last clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that idol pieces are also permitted. The משנה said 'statues' only so that its last clause about hand and foot shapes would be read correctly.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same law applies even to broken pieces of an idol. The משנה said 'pieces of statues' only because it wanted to teach the last clause: if one found the shape of a hand or a foot, they are forbidden, because things like them are worshipped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל by explaining why the משנה used the word 'statues'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both statue pieces and idol pieces are permitted. The משנה talks about plain, unknown statues so that its last clause is also about unknown objects. That teaches that an unknown hand or foot shape is forbidden even when we don't know it was worshipped.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a משנה

steps.whatToRemember: According to שמואל, pieces of both statues and idols are permitted. The משנה said 'statues' to show that a hand or foot shape is forbidden even when nobody knows it was worshipped.
steps.confusionAlert: The word 'statues' is not meant to exclude idol pieces. It was chosen for the sake of the last clause, not to limit the first one.

phrases.aramaic: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ שִׁבְרֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
phrases.english: The same is true even of broken pieces of an idol,
and the reason it teaches "broken pieces of statues"
is because it wanted to teach the last clause:
if he found the shape of a hand or the shape of a foot,
these are forbidden,
because things like them are worshipped.
phrases.notes: Because the first clause is about unknown statues, this clause is too: even an unknown hand or foot shape is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הַדִּין דַּאֲפִילּוּ שִׁבְרֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the משנה's word choice as setting up the last clause, not as limiting the first rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word 'statues' seemed to mean that pieces of a real idol are forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Idol pieces are also permitted. 'Statues' was used so the last clause would teach that even an unknown hand or foot shape is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the גמרא reads a משנה's wording: a word in the first clause may be chosen to shape how the last clause is understood.

steps.title: Why is a found hand or foot shape forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that a found hand or foot shape is forbidden and asks why. According to שמואל, broken pieces of an idol are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: If someone found the shape of a hand or the shape of a foot, these are forbidden, because things like it are worshipped. Why?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last part of the משנה and asks why a found hand or foot should be forbidden. This sets up a challenge to שמואל, and the answer comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said that even broken pieces of a real עבודה זרה are permitted. A hand or foot found on its own looks like a broken-off piece of a statue. So by שמואל's rule it should be permitted, yet the משנה forbids it.

keyTerms.meaning: Why? It often signals a challenge.

steps.confusionAlert: The question 'Why?' is not about the משנה's own reason, since the משנה already gave one. It asks how this ruling fits with שמואל, who permits broken pieces.

phrases.english: We learned in the משנה: If one found the shape of a hand
or the shape of a foot, these are forbidden,
because things like it are worshipped.
Why?
phrases.notes: He means: a lone hand or foot looks like a broken piece, and שמואל permits broken pieces, so why forbid it?

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: מָצָא תַּבְנִית יָד תַּבְנִית רֶגֶל — הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ אֲסוּרִין, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁכַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ נֶעֱבָד. אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Step 13 explained that the משנה wrote 'statues' so that its last clause would be read correctly. Now the גמרא turns to that last clause itself and challenges שמואל from it.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that even broken pieces of a known עבודה זרה are permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A found hand or foot looks like a broken-off piece. If broken pieces of an idol are permitted, this should be permitted too, yet the משנה forbids it.
